Good morning.
I'm Martin Maxa from the Department of Measurement, here at this faculty.
This is joint work with Jakub Svatoš from the same department.
Today I'll talk about detecting, classifying and localizing impulsive sounds – in our case, gunshots.
The main part is gunshot classification, where we compare different cepstral features and two classifiers.
And I'll briefly show how the system localizes the source.

Slide 2 – Motivation and research questions [0:45–1:50]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
This work is part of a larger project – an acoustic sensor system for protecting soft targets.
Acoustic detection is a good complement to cameras.
Sound is omnidirectional, and you don't need a line of sight.
[CUT] The full system has to detect an impulsive event, classify it – ideally down to the calibre – and localize the source.
And it has to work outdoors, with noise and a lot of reflections. [/CUT]
[CLICK]
In this study we ask three questions.
First, which cepstral features best separate gunshots from similar impulsive sounds?
Second, which classifier works better – a neural network or a support vector machine?
And third, how does the frame length affect the results?

Slide 3 – The acoustic signature of a gunshot [1:50–3:00]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
Let's start with the signal of a gunshot.
A gunshot has one or two components, depending on the projectile speed.
A subsonic shot has only the muzzle blast.
A supersonic one also has a shock wave.
This recording is a supersonic shot, so we can see both.
The first one, at about two and a half milliseconds, is the shock wave.
[CUT] It's created along the bullet's path and has the typical N-shape. [/CUT]
[CLICK]
The second one, about forty-five milliseconds later, is the muzzle blast.
It comes from the gases leaving the barrel, and every gunshot has it.
Everything between and after them is mostly reflections from the surroundings.
This matters for the frame length, and I'll come back to it in the results.

Slide 4 – Single-domain analysis is insufficient [3:00–3:30]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
This also shows why one domain alone is not enough.
The spectrum often tells you more about the environment than about the gunshot.
And the waveform changes as the sound travels and hits obstacles.
So we need features that combine both domains, and cepstral features do exactly that.

Slide 5 – Proposed system architecture [3:30–4:20]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
Now to the system itself.
It's a set of independent sensor units connected to a remote server.
Each unit continuously monitors its surroundings.
When it detects an impulsive event, it sends the recorded signal to the server.
The server then does two things – it classifies the event and localizes the source.
More units mean wider coverage, and they let us estimate the position of the source.
We tested the system with several calibres and types of ammunition.

Slide 6 – Localization – bearing from TDoA [4:20–5:20]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
Let me briefly explain the localization first.
Each sensor unit has two MEMS microphones, about twenty centimetres apart, sampled at 44.1 kilohertz.
We measure the time difference of arrival between the two microphones.
From this delay we get the direction to the source, using the equation here.
[CLICK]
So one unit gives us one direction.
With two units we get two directions, and where they cross is the position of the source.
We tested this on seventy events at nine reference angles.
With cross-correlation and parabolic interpolation, the mean absolute error was zero point seven seven degrees.

Slide 7 – Feature extraction – cepstral coefficients [5:20–5:50]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
Now to the main part – classification.
We compared four different cepstral feature extractors.
They all use the same chain – framing, FFT, a filter bank, then a logarithm and a DCT.
The main difference is the filter bank.
Here you can see all four filter banks on the same frequency axis.

Slide 8 – Feature extraction – the four filter banks [5:50–6:25]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
MFCC uses the mel scale, with dense filters at low frequencies.
It comes from speech processing, but it works for gunshots too.
LFCC has linearly spaced filters, and IMFCC uses an inverted mel scale, dense at high frequencies.
GTCC uses a gammatone filter bank, which is based on a model of human hearing.
It's also reported to be more robust to noise than MFCC.

Slide 10 – Classification results – MCC at a glance [6:40–7:35]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
Here are the same results, just the Matthews correlation coefficient.
MCC takes the whole confusion matrix into account, so it's less affected by class imbalance than accuracy.
The red line is GTCC.
It's on top in both panels, at every frame length.
The neural network does better than the SVM, and the gap grows with longer frames.
The best configuration is GTCC with the neural network and a fifty-millisecond frame.
That gives ninety-nine point one five percent accuracy, ninety-six point seven seven percent recall, and an MCC of zero point nine eight.
In other words, one hundred and seventeen correct decisions out of one hundred and eighteen.

Slide 11 – Discussion [7:35–8:45]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
Three things to take from this.
First, MFCC, LFCC and IMFCC give similar results, so the filter spacing makes little difference.
Second, GTCC is clearly better.
[CUT] One likely reason is that the gammatone bank comes from a hearing model and is known to be more robust to noise.
But we didn't test that directly. [/CUT]
Third, the neural network is slightly better than the SVM, especially with longer frames.
That's a general trend, not true for every single result.
[CLICK]
And finally, longer frames generally improve accuracy.
But at fifty milliseconds, the frame already contains more and more reflections, not just the gunshot itself.
So even longer frames wouldn't necessarily help.

column1:
Slide 12 – Conclusion [8:45–9:30]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
To sum up.
We presented a distributed acoustic sensor system that detects, classifies and localizes impulsive sounds.
For gunshot classification, cepstral features work well with both classifiers.
GTCC gives the best results of the four.
And the neural network is slightly better than the SVM, especially with longer frames.
All of this was tested on real firearms, with several calibres and types of ammunition.
Thank you.
